0.content: The faded colour recovery route for balanced scans (black is black, white is white, the colour has collapsed). One shot at a time, at 768 × 576 for the video model. The carrier is what the video model follows and the edges are what keeps it from moving things. Every frame keeps the scan’s brightness; only the colour is new. Yellow is the dye that fades first, so the yellow-blue choices are an interpretation, and the red-green that survived is evidence.

7.title: Diffusion reconstruction stairs kit: overlapping H3 windows and seam blend
7.content: How the stairs shot on the diffusion full reconstruction page was made. MiniMax H3 rebuilds the shot in overlapping sections at 768 × 432, because the model can only do about ten seconds at a time, and a light seam blend removes the tone steps at the cuts. On the four example windows, the seam blend matches the published result to ΔE 1.07 on average, which is smaller than you can see. The hybrid step gives identical pixels. Source and models are in the record.

9.title: Steps
9.content: . | Hybrid and median carrier. For each reference frame, run . python tools/make_hybrid.py --scan FG_01.00000200.png --telecine-dir BG_01/ --frame 200 --last-frame 624 --out hybrids/ . The 16mm frame is median-filtered (23 px) and reduced to 240 × 135 for the full canvas: the median takes out the damage, and most of the detail with it, leaving the geometry of the shot for the model to follow. The closest telecine frame within ±12 frames is registered into it, tone-matched and feathered in. If the registration doesn’t line up, choose another frame. On frame 200 of the stairs shot this gives the same pixels as the published hybrid. | Reference still. Give an image generator the hybrid (Image 1) and one finished still from the shot (Image 2, look only) with the prompt in reference/reference_prompt.txt; replace {FRAME} and {CONTENT}. The stills used for the published shot were made with ChatGPT image generation, which is not an open model, so this step cannot be repeated exactly. Check each still against its hybrid and throw out any where people or architecture have moved; the still sets the look, and the model will follow its geometry too. The stills used are in example/. | Generate each window. Load one of the _ui.json graphs in graphs/ (laid out, with notes on what the window does and what should and should not happen; the matching .json without the suffix is the same graph in API format), point it at the matching example/ source MP4 and three reference stills, and run. The graphs are for this stairs shot: w1 (frames 1–243), w2b (128–370), w3b (300–542) and w3 (382–624). Start each section in a calm passage; the model gets lost if it starts in the middle of a movement. The kit already includes the four H3 windows used for the check (example/w1.mp4 and so on), so you can skip steps 1–3 if you only want to try the join. | Seam blend. From this folder: . INPUT_DIR=example OUTPUT_DIR=out python tools/run_blend_example.py . It uses the overlaps to remove the tone steps at cuts 200, 340 and 400 (half-pool 12, dissolve 12). The windows don’t always agree with each other, so the join is made where they do and dissolved over a few frames. For your own shot, change the windows and cuts in run_blend_example.py. | .

18.title: Your own frames
18.content: Upload your frame as the source. Keep the chart. For the edge map, either make one with OpenCV (cv2.Canny(grey, 80, 160)) and upload it, or use the Detect edges node already in the graph: drag its output into Scale edge map in place of the uploaded edge map. ComfyUI’s edge detector is close to OpenCV’s but not identical, so results differ a little from this test; for your own frames that does not matter. What comes out of the model is an interpretation. Compare the composite with the source at full size: a face that has changed, an object that wasn’t there, colour crossing an edge, clipped highlights and a change in the grain are the usual failures. Nothing in the frame proves what the original colour was.

23.title: Diffusion healing: the second pass
23.content: The last step of the flute players shot on the diffusion healing page. The first pass (MiniMax H3, with the film’s own drumming kept where H3 couldn’t follow it) leaves two kinds of picture side by side: the model’s and the film’s. A light Wan VACE pass makes them one picture. Nothing should move: the geometry and the motion come out exactly as they went in, and only the look is made consistent. On the example files it matches the published result to ΔE 0.9 on average, and each window to ΔE 0.6 or better, which is smaller than you can see. Source, first pass and models are in the record.

25.content: . | Second pass. Load graph/second_pass_vace_refine_ui.json (laid out, with notes on what the pass does and what should and should not change; second_pass_vace_refine.json is the same graph in API format), point the Load Video node at one 81-frame window of your first pass, and run. It encodes the window as the starting point and samples at denoise 0.30 (seed 0, 30 steps, CFG 4.5), with the same window as the VACE control. The low denoise is the point: the model is only allowed to change the picture a little, so it smooths the join between the two kinds of picture and can’t redraw anything. Run it once for each window. Each window overlaps the next by 30 frames, which is what the seam blend uses. | Pack each window. The graph saves PNG frames. 31.title: Digitization: First Scan, Last Chance
31.content: Digitisation is the moment the picture leaves its fragile physical container. The scan is the foundation of every restoration step that follows, so it should not be a quick transfer or a creative grade baked in. For damaged or rare material the first scan may also be the only one: the film may not survive being handled again, the budget may not stretch to a second pass, or the decay may get there first. Everything on this site works with the scan as it is, because most of the time the scan is all that is left. Article image from "First Scan, Last Chance": digitisation as the moment the picture is separated from its fragile film container. The aim is to capture as much of the picture as the film still holds, in RGB and in brightness. A good scan keeps the film’s dynamic range, the separation between the colour channels, the variation in density, the grain and the texture, so that whatever comes later has something to work with. A poor scan throws evidence away for good: clipped highlights, crushed shadows, a bad white balance, automatic exposure decisions or a clipped channel can’t be reliably put back afterwards. The scanner's exposure and RGB controls decide how much usable picture gets captured before restoration even begins. Digitisation choices should be tested against the film element and what you are preserving it for, not treated as one colour path that fits everything. Scanning principles: . | Capture a preservation-grade scan before any restoration decision gets baked in. | No clipped highlights, no crushed shadows, no automatic white balance, no heavy noise reduction, no sharpening, no creative LUTs at capture. | Watch the RGB parade, the waveform, the histogram and channel clipping during setup and during the capture itself. | Do a first pass to find the sequence’s tonal extremes, density shifts, splice flashes, severe fading, and any scanner setting that is going to fail. | Write down the scanner model, gate, optics, resolution, bit depth, colour encoding, transforms, exposure settings, and any wet-gate or cleanup choices. | Keep the raw scan or archival master separate from restoration renders, review proxies and creative grades. | . | Risk during digitization | Why it matters later | . | Clipped highlights or channels | Picture gone for good, and colour recovery, deflicker, dust removal and grading all have less to work with. | . | Incorrect white point | Adds a false colour relationship that restoration tools may learn or amplify. | . | Automatic scanner decisions | Can change from shot to shot, giving you flicker, unstable density or a channel balance that wanders. | . | Baked creative grade | Narrows the evidence left for a future restoration or a different interpretation. | . | Low bit depth / compressed delivery format | Loses the subtle density and colour information that restoration needs, especially in faded material. | . For historical or deteriorated material, go for a conservative, high-bit-depth scan that keeps everything the scanner captured, and make the restoration choices afterwards, in post, where they can be undone. ADX, Cineon, linear, ACES and display-referred workflows all have their place, but test them against the actual film element rather than assume one is right. For this colour-recovery method the one rule is continuity: whatever scan and transform path you choose, Source and Reference go into training with the same transforms, written down. Digitisation, restoration and remastering are three different things. Digitisation turns the film into data. Restoration deals with the damage or loss that came from the physical container. Remastering adapts the work for a new display, release or audience. Keep those lines visible in the metadata, so whoever comes later knows which decisions came from the object, which from the restoration and which from the delivery master. Source article and images: First Scan, Last Chance: The Critical Role of Digitization in Preserving Film Heritage.

32.title: Why Faded Scans Turn Magenta
32.content: Colour film records the picture in subtractive dye layers. When those dyes no longer have the density they had, the scan no longer carries even RGB information. The common failure is the pink or magenta cast: the cyan and yellow dyes weaken against the magenta, so red and blue dominate and the green channel loses its useful separation. For this workflow the point is practical, not aesthetic: the magenta picture usually still has usable brightness, texture and grain, but its colour channels are biased, compressed or partly clipped. A neutral pre-balance gives CopyCat a cleaner input to start from before the colour comes in from the reference. Faded scan with a strong red/magenta bias. A technical red compression and rebalance, to give the model a cleaner input. The Resolve parade scope showing channel imbalance in faded film. The goal is a technical pre-balance, not a final creative grade. The faded scan in Resolve, before balancing. The same scan after a neutral, technical balance. What is going on in the film . What is failing: in chromogenic film the picture is made of cyan, magenta and yellow dye clouds, one on top of the other, in gelatin layers. These organic dyes don’t age at the same rate. When the cyan and the yellow fade faster than the magenta, the balance shifts towards pink, purple or magenta. NARA’s inspection guidance says exactly this: magenta film has faded because the cyan and yellow dye layers have weakened and the magenta is left dominant. The NFPF describes the same pattern for modern colour motion picture film: spontaneous chemical changes in the image dyes, often with a purplish cast from the cyan and yellow going first. Why it happened: not a bad scan or a bad grade, though either can make it look worse. It is chemical deterioration that has been going on for decades: broken bonds in the dyes, dyes of unequal stability, heat, humidity, light, time and the storage history. Graphics Atlas notes that chromogenic dyes fade in the dark as well as in the light; cyan fading in dark storage can leave the whole picture magenta. Older chromogenic stocks and prints, especially mid-century material from before the stability improvements, are more vulnerable than modern stocks. Why ordinary grading isn’t enough: an RGB grade can rebalance the channels globally, but it can’t bring back colour that isn’t there any more, or that has been compressed into contaminated channel relationships. Recent digital unfading research treats this as a reconstruction problem, limited by what dye is left, the quality of the scan and the references you have. Severe cases need informed inference: a direct reference, a constructed one, spectral or density analysis, documented memory colour, or a model trained on pairs. Data worth capturing before restoration: . | Data | Why it helps | . | Stock, generation, and approximate date | Tells you how much the dyes were at risk and which chromogenic process it is likely to be. | . | Storage history | Heat, humidity and light explain how fast it faded and in what pattern. | . | Physical inspection | Separates dye fading from vinegar syndrome, dirt, shrinkage, mould, mechanical damage or emulsion problems. | . | RGB parade scopes / histograms | Shows channel compression, clipping and separation before and after the pre-balance. | . | Dmin/Dmax or neutral patches when available | Measures the density loss and the contamination in highlights and shadows. | . | Reference comparison | A DVD, a telecine, another print, artwork or a constructed reference: what separates evidence from somebody’s opinion. | . | Transform log | The scanner settings, ODT, colour space, pre-balance, cleanup and clamp choices before CopyCat. | . How this workflow deals with it: first deal with the film itself: cool, dry storage, inspection, cleaning, and a scan before the decay goes any further. Then a technical, non-creative pre-balance to take the worst of the cast off and give Nuke a more useful source. In colour recovery CopyCat doesn’t replace the picture: it keeps the source’s brightness and detail and learns to rebuild the Cb and Cr from an aligned or constructed reference. If a channel is biased but still carries information, the pre-balance may get a lot back. If the colour is genuinely gone, the recovery depends on outside evidence and has to be written down as an interpretation. Technical references: . | National Archives - Motion Picture Film Condition Assessment | National Film Preservation Foundation - Color Dye Fading | Graphics Atlas - Chromogenic deterioration | Heritage, 2023 - Digital Unfading of Chromogenic Film Informed by Its Spectral Densities | National Film Preservation Foundation - The Film Preservation Guide | .

34.title: Preparing Reliable Training Pairs
34.content: The model learns whatever is in the training pairs, so a bad pair gives you a bad result. Each pair has to show the same moment in the faded scan and the better reference. This is simple when both scans come from the same element. It is harder with a telecine, a broadcast master or a home-video release, which can differ in edits, cadence, framing, distortion and missing frames.

35.title: What counts as a good pair
35.content: A good pair: . | shows the same moment in both images; | has edges and moving subjects in the same places; | is not from a fade, dissolve, splice or a different shot; | has a reference that is better for the task; | has not had faces, bodies or objects stretched by the alignment; | still matches once the aligned files are rendered. | . If you are not sure about a pair, drop it. A few pairs you trust beat a big set with mistakes in it.

36.title: Preparation sequence
36.content: . | Get to know both elements. Write down frame rate, dimensions, pixel shape, field order, where the reels change and any editorial differences you already know about. | Find the rough match first. Work out how the two line up overall before you solve individual shots. | Then go shot by shot. One offset almost never describes a whole historical transfer. | Try the simplest alignment first. Translation, scale, rotation and a modest affine correction are easier to understand than a complex warp, and easier to spot when they go wrong. | Bring in the heavier methods only when they clearly help. Perspective correction or feature matching can save a difficult shot, but a solver’s result still has to be looked at. | Render the candidates. Judge the files the model will actually see, not the alignment controls. | Check motion and shot boundaries. A matching background can hide a moving face, hand or object that is one frame out of time. | Keep only the pairs you have checked. Write down what you threw out and why, rather than filling the gaps with generated or interpolated “ground truth.” | Review the whole selection. Contact sheets and difference views show repeated frames, coverage gaps and outliers. | .

37.title: Why motion needs special attention
37.content: Two frames can match in the background while a person in the foreground is one frame off. A model trained on that pair learns the error. Check the moving areas, compare each candidate with its neighbouring frames, and remove pairs near uncertain cuts. Difficult shots can use stronger alignment, but they get the same final review.

38.title: What should be saved
38.content: A training set someone can reuse needs, alongside it: . | the identity of every source and reference frame; | the pairs kept and the pairs dropped, with the reasons; | the alignment method used for each pair kept; | a visual review sheet; | file counts and checksums; | the crop, colour transforms, and frame ranges used in Nuke; | enough information to return from an output frame to its original source. | . These records let another person trace what the model learned from and remove a bad example later.

39.title: Long references that drift
39.content: On a long reference with timing drift, shot changes and difficult foreground motion, start with a conservative alignment of the whole sequence, then add pairs for the shots that are under-represented, without lowering the bar for what counts as a good pair. The number of pairs on its own tells you nothing: coverage, where each frame came from, whether the rendered files are intact and a look at the moving subjects all have to check out before a dataset is ready. Another film may need fewer pairs, more pairs, or a different balance between one model for the sequence and models per shot.

40.title: When to train by shot
40.content: Start with one model for the whole sequence when the material hangs together. It has more examples to learn from and there is less to manage. Go to a model per shot only after you have looked at the sequence result and found shots the shared model can’t do well. Reuse the pairs you already checked for those shots, keep the complete source range for inference, and compare the shot model’s result against the sequence model before you replace it.

41.title: Automation and review
41.content: Automation can suggest matches, align images and organise files. Whether a pair goes in is a restoration decision: someone looks at it, and the decision is written down so it can be revisited.

45.title: Black-and-white colourization
45.content: Colourization is a different thing from the rest of this site: there was never any colour on the film, so everything here is an interpretation, and every page says so. What can be done is to make the interpretation agree with the film. A black-and-white stock doesn’t see brightness the way the eye does; it records according to its own spectral sensitivity, so the greys on the film are a measurement, and any colour put on them has to be a colour that stock would have recorded as exactly those greys. Every result here is rebuilt that way, whole shots at a time, with the picture untouched. Reveal The General (1926), Annabelle in the garden, 124 frames at full resolution. The picture is untouched; only the colour was added. Record

46.title: Orthochromatic and panchromatic film
46.content: . | Orthochromatic stock is sensitive to blue and green but almost blind to red. It was the normal negative until the mid-1920s: red lips and ruddy skin record dark, blue skies and blue eyes record pale. | Panchromatic stock sees the whole visible range, but more blue and less red than the eye. It became standard for features around 1926–1928, often shot with filters outdoors. | . Treat either as ordinary video brightness and the colour comes out wrong in predictable places. A red dress on orthochromatic film can rightly come out lighter than it looks in the scan, because the film never recorded its red.

47.title: How it works
47.content: Only public-domain or rights-cleared scans are used for this. Qwen Image Edit 2511 makes a few colour frames from the shot itself, on the exact source picture, checked at full size. MiniMax H3, with the Fun ControlNet where the movement needs it, carries them through the shot; on a pan it gets several anchors so it stays on course. Then, once per film, a choice is made of how much red, green and blue the stock recorded, and the colour is rebuilt so that the stock would have recorded exactly the greyscale on the film. The whole frame is processed the same way, no masks, no local fixes. Then review: full-size crops, frame-to-frame strips, skin and foliage at normal speed.

56.title: Building the Colour Target
56.content: This is the stage for the common case: the scan still has its detail but the colour has faded or shifted, and a better copy of the same frames has the colour. Do the preparation and alignment stages first. Training, inference and delivery are on Training, Inference and Review.

57.title: Record the reference
57.content: Write down which edition the reference is, who owns or supplied it, its transforms, its compression, the crop, and how far it could be aligned. A DVD, a telecine, another print or a video master all work, as long as it shows the same frames with better colour.

58.title: Build the target
58.content: The training target is the source’s brightness with the reference’s colour. That is the whole trick: the model learns colour only, and never gets the chance to replace the scan’s detail. | If the reference is compressed video, a restrained median or debanding pass helps. Write down what you did. | Clone the aligned reference crop onto the source so both branches use the same picture area. | Convert source and reference from the working space to YCbCr. | In a Shuffle, map: . | red from Source red (Y); | green from Reference green (Cb); | blue from Reference blue (Cr); | alpha to black. | . | Convert the target from YCbCr back to the working space. | Clamp input and target to the expected range, remove alpha, and copy the same bounding box to both. | Connect the prepared source as CopyCat input and the combined image as target. | . CopyCat training layout with YCbCr channel separation. The chroma target uses Source Y with Reference Cb and Cr.

59.title: Checks
59.content: . | Difference the input and the target in YCbCr. The luminance should be nearly identical; if it isn’t, the reference’s brightness has got in. | Check that the paired crops and bounding boxes match. | Drop a frame if an alignment error could be learned as a colour edge. | During review, watch for hue drift, colour bleeding, unstable skin tones and flicker. | In Resolve, put the recovered render above the original with Composite Mode set to Color when the delivery needs the source brightness protected explicitly. | . Candy Candy training checkpoints. The colour came from the PAL DVD.

60.title: Troubleshooting
60.content: | Problem | Check | . | Detail becomes softer | Check that Source Y, not Reference Y, is going into the target | . | Wrong hue or colour bleeding | Go back over the YCbCr mapping, the alignment, the crop and the reference transforms | . | Flicker between frames | Add pairs around the transition and check whether the reference itself is consistent there | . | Model misses a colour family | Add well-aligned pairs that contain that colour; training longer won’t invent it | . 62.title: Faded colour recovery
62.content: Colour recovery is the main thread of this research. The case that matters most is the one that keeps coming up in Latin America and Southeast Asia: the magenta scan, or the red scan, is the only thing left of the film. There is no negative to go back to, no better print, no DVD. Whatever a spectral scanner might get out of the element, you don’t have the element. So everything here works with the scan as it is right now. The idea is simple to say. Don’t add anything, don’t clean the film, don’t make it HD. Just get the colour back. The scan keeps its own brightness, grain and damage, and only the colour is rebuilt, frame after frame, through the whole shot. Reveal Counter Attack (1976), crowd shot. A film copy faded to red, 385 frames with a fast pan; the recovered colour on the scan's own brightness. Record

63.title: How it works
63.content: The first problem is getting one good colour frame. A lot of prompts and workflows were tested for this before one recipe came out that most consistently gives an acceptable colour. Qwen Image Edit gets the faded frame, an edge map of that frame, and a softly blurred colour chart, so it has nothing to copy except colour. The result is checked at full size. If it doesn’t pass, nothing else happens on that shot. The second problem is the real one: temporal consistency. You could just run that image model 24 times a second, but these models make a different decision every time they run, so you end up with 24 different decisions every second. Fine for a thumbnail, useless for a film. What carries the colour through the shot is MiniMax H3, a video model, with Alibaba’s Fun ControlNet. The ControlNet is what makes the model behave: it follows the edges of every frame, so the people stay where they are and only the colour changes. That works on crowds, pans, hands and changing light, up to a point, and when the model gets lost the shot is done in sections, which means running more inference than you would like. The frames that pass review then teach a small model built for this, the Temporal CbCr adapter. It learns the colour of that one shot in about 90 seconds and colours every frame consistently. Finally the colour goes back onto the scan. Only the chroma is taken; the luma, which is where the resolution and the grain live, is the film’s, at the scan’s full size. We are not very sensitive to the resolution of colour, so even if the model saw a reduced picture, the result doesn’t look reduced. Some scans arrive already balanced (black is black, white is white, and the colour has collapsed to almost nothing). Those go through the same route with one rule added: the red-green colour that survived in the dyes is kept and may only be strengthened, never flipped. Yellow is the dye that fades first, so the yellow-blue axis is what the recovery has to supply.

66.title: What works and what doesn’t
66.content: In June the result was a single still, and anything that moved flickered. By September there were whole shots with pans, crowds and dancing: the ballroom, the crowd, the waterfront, the quarry. Every faded shot tried so far has come back, given enough passes. Hard motion is not a wall any more; it is sections, review and the adapter, and time. Time is the honest cost. The first whole shot took four hours of TeleStyle. H3 with the ControlNet does a 124-frame section in 20 to 45 minutes on an RTX 5090, and you waste inference, because out of a 200-frame run you may only keep 50 and go again. The adapter trains in about 90 seconds, which is why it finishes everything. Is it production ready? Not yet. The target is three out of four new shots right on the first pass, and some still need a second. Deep shadows keep a tint on the hardest shots. And the colour is an interpretation unless a surviving reference confirms it; every page here says so. The goal at the beginning was an app where you upload a shot and get it back in colour. That is technically possible now, but these films need care, and the decisions are still too many to leave unattended.

86.title: Diffusion healing
86.content: Sometimes part of a film is simply gone. A stretch of nitrate has decayed to nothing, a negative has a gap of fifteen frames while the sound runs on, the emulsion is breaking up across the whole frame. If you know the tools we use, Phoenix, DIAMANT, PFClean, DRS Nova, you know that two or three frames is about the limit of what they can interpolate, and even those don’t look that good. Fifteen frames is out of the question, because the tools only have the frames around the gap to copy from. The information is lost. So this is the experimental end of the research: can a video model fill the gap? The rule is that everything that survives, in every element of the film, is used first. The model generates only what is missing, it is steered by the movement before and after, and every generated pixel is on record. The point is a reconstruction you cannot tell from the film. Which is also a concern, and the reason this work is part of the Trust in Archives initiative. Reveal Knights of the Trail, nitrate, frames 734–959. The scan plays to its worst frame, holds, and heals: the cowboy, his hands and the bag are the film's in every frame, and only the ruined background is generated. Courtesy of the George Eastman Museum. Record Healing covers specific defects, missing areas, partial frames and bounded frame gaps when substantial usable picture survives. Whole-shot regeneration where most picture evidence is unusable belongs to Diffusion Full Reconstruction. Reference-based resolution/detail enhancement belongs to the new Diffusion Upscaling idea. See project names.

87.title: How it works
87.content: When several elements of the same film exist, they are lined up and the undamaged one is chosen frame by frame. For Knights of the Trail that was a nitrate print and a diacetate safety copy, and even the safety copy had frames missing, because by the time it was made the nitrate was already going and they cut those parts out. So the shot’s timeline becomes a map: which element each frame comes from, and where nothing survives. Inside the gaps a video model generates the missing picture. The original idea, from before any of these models existed, was a skeleton: follow the movement before the gap and after it, interpolate the movement across it, and put a texture on top. That is basically what happens. H3 wouldn’t do it, because in reference mode it wants to modify everything in between, but Wan VACE, an older model, can be bounded by the frames around the gap and fill only that. Everything outside the gap stays original, and fast thin action the model would redraw, a hand, a drumstick, stays the film’s wherever the film still carries it. Generated frames and regions are an inference, not a recovery, and the record says exactly where they are.

89.title: What works and what doesn’t
89.content: The Knights of the Trail shot went through six versions, each one closer to the rule that what moves stays the film’s. If that shot were shown on its own, could you tell which part is generated? Probably not, and that is the point. A fifteen-frame hole in the camera negative of Poison Pen (1939), from a commercial job, is being filled the same way, with the actors’ movement tracked across the gap. The Wong shot is the frontier: the emulsion is breaking up across the whole frame, so there is no clean element to prefer. It proved the method and stops at a good result at working size, to be finished together with conventional restoration. Working size is the general limit right now. These models run at around 768 × 560 and about ten seconds at a time, so shots are done in overlapping windows and the original-resolution pass is a separate, final step. None of this is a one-click application. It is a lot of curation, a lot of iterations, and the models don’t always agree with each other, so it is closer to a VFX job done case by case than to a filter. And a search for public-domain footage with loss on this scale, through 847 films in public archives, found none, which is why these examples come from collections rather than from the trailer reel used elsewhere on the site.

93.title: Diffusion reconstruction
93.content: This started as an upscaling project, and upscaling is still not quite the right word for it. El Tinterillo survives as a 16mm print with everything wrong with it: frames stuck together, dirt, the emulsion damaged, and a telecine with no resolution and a crop, made close enough to the original that at least the picture is clean. If you try normal restoration tools on the print you can’t even start, because there is not enough spatial or temporal information left to borrow from. So this calls for a different approach. A video model rebuilds the picture from what survives, following the structure and the movement of the two elements. That is not film restoration in the proper sense: the result is based on an interpretation, a restorer’s and the model’s, of how an image of this era should look, and the fine detail is filled from the model’s training, not from the film. It is a reconstruction, and it is labelled as one. But for this kind of footage there is no other way, and it is better than nothing. Reveal El Tinterillo, shot FG02, 410 frames. The damaged 16mm print, and the shot rebuilt by MiniMax H3 from the print, the telecine and one look reference. Record Current scope: whole-shot diffusion when all or most surviving picture evidence is unusable in its current state. Diffusion Healing repairs specific losses when substantial usable evidence survives. Diffusion Upscaling is the separate reference-based video enhancement idea. Historical Tinterillo upscaling records belong to Full Reconstruction. See project names.

94.title: How it works
94.content: First the two elements are combined into a hybrid: the telecine goes inside, the 16mm print around it, so you get the full frame with the best of both. Then a strong median, which is like a blur but really an average of the pixels around each point, takes out the damage. It also takes out all the fine detail, so what is left is the geometry of the shot, a baseline the model can follow. From that comes a synthetic reference: one still that sets how the picture should look, and the same still for every shot of the reel, so the whole film comes out with one look. MiniMax H3 in reference mode then generates the shot in windows of about ten seconds, each starting in a calm passage. The windows don’t always agree with each other, so the frames where they do are joined with a short blend. Unlike colour recovery, where the film’s luma is kept and only the chroma is taken, here the luma is beyond saving and the model’s picture is what there is. It has a more plastic quality than film. It is double synthetic, if you like.

96.title: What works and what doesn’t
96.content: Five shots of El Tinterillo are finished with the same method and the same look. Small faces and lip movement are the weak point, because the model works at 768 × 432; a test showed the detail is there in the source, so the limit is in how the model is guided, not in the film, and the lips are the next pass. The obvious things were tried first and dropped: video upscalers (SeedVR2, FlashVSR), Wan VACE driven by the source, a CopyCat detail model. None of them suited this material. What works is windows, and making the windows agree with each other, which wastes inference and takes iterations. Maybe somebody has a more straightforward way; at the moment this is the only one that works here. The original scan and every raw window are kept, and the result is labelled as a reconstruction.

109.title: De CopyCat a los modelos de pesos abiertos
109.content: Mi investigación empezó con CopyCat, dentro de Nuke. La idea es entrenar un modelo pequeño para cada película a partir de fotogramas equivalentes de dos copias: el escaneo dañado y una copia mejor de la misma película que muestra el resultado que queremos. Eso es lo que presenté el año pasado en Roma, y sigue siendo mi punto de partida. Pero necesita esa copia mejor para aprender, y es una plataforma cerrada hecha para efectos visuales. Desde entonces, los modelos de pesos abiertos, los que cualquiera puede descargar y ejecutar, se han vuelto lo bastante buenos para imagen, video y voz en una sola estación de trabajo. La gente ya los usa para “restaurar” fotos antiguas y películas caseras, pero casi siempre fuera del archivo. Así que mi pregunta es: ¿cómo los acotamos para que sean útiles para el trabajo que realmente necesitamos? . Diapositiva 3 .

110.title: Ocultar frente a recuperar
110.content: La mayoría de las herramientas de restauración usan filtros espaciales y temporales. Toman imagen prestada del mismo fotograma o de los fotogramas de alrededor, y cuando no hay nada limpio que copiar, interpolan. La diapositiva muestra Dry Clean en Phoenix sobre Point Blank (1967); las marcas rojas son lo que detectó y eliminó. Estas herramientas pueden ocultar polvo, rayas y parpadeo, y cubrir dos o tres fotogramas faltantes. Pero no pueden traer de vuelta lo que se perdió. Si somos honestos, la restauración digital siempre ha consistido en ocultar, no en recuperar. Así que la IA en restauración no es algo completamente nuevo. Lo que nos da es una forma de abordar problemas que antes no eran posibles ni técnica ni económicamente, trabajando con el escaneo tal como está. En muchos archivos, sobre todo en América Latina y el Sudeste Asiático, ese escaneo desvanecido es lo único que queda de una película. 113.title: Crear una referencia sintética
113.content: ¿Y qué pasa cuando no hay referencia? Creas una: un fotograma de color aprobado para cada plano. Lo llamo referencia sintética, y la hago con Qwen Image Edit, un modelo de imagen de pesos abiertos de Alibaba. Mi primer intento fue guiarlo con una leader lady, la mujer de los fotogramas de calibración al comienzo de un rollo. No funcionó. Estos modelos no entienden el significado como nosotros, así que en vez de tomar solo el color, el modelo mezcló las dos imágenes y la mujer terminó dentro del plano. A eso lo llamo contaminación semántica. Una carta de color simple funcionó mejor, una vez que la desenfoqué un poco. Guía el color sin darle al modelo nada más que copiar. Luego vino el prompt, que es la forma de hablarle al modelo. Hice un pequeño concurso, al que llamé America's Next Top Machine Learning Model: decenas de prompts y cientos de fotogramas de prueba, en siete rondas sobre siete películas desvanecidas. Un prompt solo pasaba una ronda si ocho de cada diez fotogramas eran aceptables. La fila inferior de la diapositiva muestra un fotograma desvanecido de Counter Attack, una película china de 1976, con tres de los finalistas. El ganador, Clara, es el que más uso, pero también uso los otros, según el plano. De la referencia sintética me quedo solo con el color. El brillo sigue viniendo del escaneo. 114.title: Mantener el color estable a lo largo de un plano
114.content: Conseguir un fotograma convincente ya no es lo difícil. Si simplemente ejecutas el modelo 24 veces por segundo, no funciona, porque estos modelos no son deterministas: cada ejecución es un poco una ruleta. Cada fotograma recibe una interpretación ligeramente distinta, y el color parpadea. La diapositiva 8 muestra una escena de baile de Obsession en la que cada fotograma se recuperó por separado. Mira el vestido de la mujer de la derecha, y el fondo. Cada fotograma es una interpretación razonable por sí solo, pero juntos no coinciden. Un buen fotograma es una miniatura. Una restauración necesita que todo el plano sea coherente consigo mismo. Eso es la consistencia temporal, y fue el mayor obstáculo. 115.title: Hacerlo más rápido: H3 y ControlNet
115.content: Tenía un color que se mantenía, pero tomaba demasiado tiempo. A finales de julio, MiniMax lanzó H3, un modelo de video muy bueno con imágenes de referencia. En una sola pasada, lleva el color aprobado a lo largo de toda una sección de un plano. Pero por sí solo, H3 se aleja de la imagen y pierde la geometría. Así que tuve que ejecutarlo en secciones cortas y hacer que todas coincidieran, lo que significaba más procesamiento y más tiempo. Luego, en agosto, Alibaba PAI lanzó un ControlNet para H3. Un ControlNet es una forma de dirigir lo que hace el modelo; este le pasa los bordes de cada fotograma, lo que ayuda a conservar la geometría y el movimiento propios de la película. Me quedo solo con el color y lo pongo sobre el brillo original, así que el grano, la aspereza, incluso la suciedad, se mantienen. Si los dejas solos, estos modelos quieren cambiarlo todo y darle un aspecto plástico. Reproducir · 0:13 Diapositiva 11 · Counter Attack: H3 + ControlNet, terminado con el adaptador Temporal CbCr . El color viene de H3 con el ControlNet, y se termina con el adaptador Temporal CbCr, que explico en la siguiente sección. Elegí este plano porque es difícil: mucho movimiento, una multitud que cambia todo el tiempo y un paneo rápido en el medio. Lo que funcionóEl color se mantiene a pesar de todo ese movimiento, y la geometría sigue igual que en el original. LimitacionesSi miras de cerca, hay algo de tinte en las sombras. Mi copia era de 30 fotogramas por segundo con una cadencia rota, así que sacar fotogramas limpios de ella fue difícil, y el adaptador necesita fotogramas bien alineados. 116.title: El adaptador Temporal CbCr
116.content: Esta es la idea detrás de mi trabajo con CopyCat, llevada fuera de Nuke para que la investigación pueda funcionar en una plataforma abierta. CbCr son los dos canales de color de una imagen de video, separados de su brillo. Ejecuto H3 o TeleStyle una o dos veces, según la duración del plano, y me quedo solo con los fotogramas que pasan la revisión. Los llamo maestros. No tienen que cubrir todo el plano, siempre que su geometría coincida con la imagen. Un modelo pequeño, con menos de un millón de parámetros, aprende el color del plano a partir de los maestros en minutos. Luego completa los fotogramas que no tienen maestro y mantiene el color estable en todo el plano. En la diapositiva 12, el primer y el tercer fotograma no tienen maestro, y el segundo y el cuarto sí. 117.title: Escalado por difusión*
117.content: * En la charla usé el nombre anterior, diffusion upscaling. Este trabajo sobre el plano completo de Tinterillo se llama ahora Diffusion Full Reconstruction. Diffusion Upscaling es una idea nueva y separada para aumentar la resolución y el detalle del vídeo con referencias. Hasta aquí, el modelo solo agrega color y el escaneo conserva su propia imagen. Pero a veces el elemento que sobrevive no tiene suficiente información para una restauración tradicional. Nuestras herramientas toman prestado del mismo fotograma o de los fotogramas de alrededor, y cuando todos los fotogramas están dañados, no queda nada que tomar. El escalado por difusión permite que un modelo de video reconstruya la imagen a partir de lo que sobrevive, siguiendo su estructura y su movimiento. De El Tinterillo solo sobreviven una copia de 16mm dañada y un telecine más limpio, pero blando, recortado y con la cadencia extraña de los telecines de esa época. Suavicé el 16mm con un filtro de mediana y luego combiné los dos, con el telecine en el centro y el 16mm alrededor. Eso da un contorno aproximado para guiar la geometría, pero el filtro también elimina el detalle fino. Así que, para definir cómo debía verse la imagen, hice otras referencias sintéticas con ChatGPT Images. Luego MiniMax H3, en modo referencia, usa esas referencias, con el clip del telecine para el movimiento, para generar cada sección del plano. Reproducir · 0:26 Diapositiva 15 · El Tinterillo: escalado por difusión, las escaleras . El escaneo original de 16mm está a la izquierda, y el resultado que aprobé, a la derecha. Llegar hasta aquí tomó un largo proceso de iteración. Lo que funcionóLa imagen de este escaneo no se puede salvar con herramientas tradicionales. H3 llena esos vacíos y reconstruye la imagen, siguiendo la estructura y el movimiento del original. LimitacionesEl resultado es en parte sintético: el modelo inventa detalle fino que la película ya no tiene, y eso hay que declararlo. El modelo trabajó a 768 × 432. Todavía hay un salto de brillo en el primer fotograma, y las caras y el detalle fino siguen siendo débiles. Algunas personas dirán que esto es una herejía, y en cierta medida lo es. Yo mismo no lo llamaría una restauración de película propiamente dicha. 118.title: Reconstrucción por difusión*
118.content: * En la charla usé el nombre anterior, diffusion reconstruction. Este trabajo de reparación de huecos y partes de fotogramas se llama ahora Diffusion Healing: sobrevive mucha imagen utilizable y la difusión repara pérdidas concretas. Diffusion Full Reconstruction es el proyecto separado de regeneración del plano completo. A veces la imagen no está dañada, sino que ya no existe: faltan fotogramas en el único elemento que sobrevive. Esto pasa mucho con el nitrato, cuando se cortó una sección en descomposición para que no dañara el resto del rollo. Herramientas como Phoenix, DIAMANT o DaVinci Resolve pueden cubrir dos o tres fotogramas faltantes con flujo óptico. En un hueco más largo, el movimiento empieza a sentirse raro, porque solo pueden interpolar lo que sobrevive. En la charla, el ejemplo es un hueco de 15 fotogramas en un negativo de cámara en el que el sonido sí sobrevive, así que hay que llenar el hueco para mantener juntos imagen y sonido. Hice el seguimiento de los actores desde el último fotograma antes del hueco hasta el primero después de él, y llevé ese movimiento a través de los fotogramas faltantes: esos son los esqueletos de la diapositiva 16. Luego el modelo de video VACE de Alibaba generó la imagen, guiado por ese movimiento, solo dentro del hueco. Lo que funcionó, y las limitaciones. Los fotogramas generados se sostienen bien, y todos los fotogramas originales quedan intactos. El límite de resolución de la diapositiva 4 sigue vigente, y lo que se genera hay que declararlo. El clip que se muestra en la diapositiva 17 no está incluido en esta página. Diapositivas 18–19 .

119.title: Combinar fuentes y luego reconstruir
119.content: Cuando sobreviven varios elementos, cada uno suele estar dañado en lugares distintos. En la charla lo mostré con una película muda que sobrevive como una copia en nitrato y una copia de seguridad en diacetato. Juntas cubren la mayor parte de la película, pero en algunos lugares el nitrato se ha descompuesto y a la copia de seguridad también le faltan esos fotogramas. Primero, junto los dos elementos. Tenían color, deformación y encuadre distintos, así que cada fotograma de uno se empareja con el otro por sus rasgos y se deforma hasta encajar. Luego, una sola corrección de tono, ajustada sobre los fotogramas equivalentes más limpios, les da a ambos el mismo aspecto. Después, cada fotograma sale del elemento que haya sobrevivido sin daño. Una línea de tiempo del plano funciona como un mapa de esto: de qué elemento sale cada fotograma y dónde no sobrevive ninguno. En esos fotogramas enmascaro solo las zonas dañadas, y Wan VACE 14B, el modelo de video de Alibaba, reconstruye solo esas zonas. La imagen que sobrevive sigue siendo original, porque no queremos reemplazar un fotograma entero solo porque una parte esté dañada. Qué funcionó y los límites. El resultado se sostiene bien, y todo lo que sobrevive queda intacto. Fue una prueba de trabajo a resolución reducida, no una restauración nativa en HD. El ejemplo de la charla no se muestra en esta página. Diapositiva 20 .

120.title: Recuperación de diálogos
120.content: La misma idea se aplica al sonido: una palabra muy distorsionada se puede reconstruir con la propia voz del actor. Usé Fish Audio S2 Pro, un modelo de voz de pesos abiertos, ejecutado en local. Se le dan unos segundos de diálogo limpio del mismo actor en la película, unos diez segundos en este caso, y las palabras exactas. Genera muchas tomas de la frase completa. El reconocimiento de voz y la comparación de voces ayudan a ordenarlas, pero lo que decide es la escucha. Luego solo se reemplaza la parte dañada, aquí alrededor de un tercio de segundo. Todo lo demás es la banda sonora original. Limitaciones. La salida del modelo era tan limpia que no se integraba, así que agregué algo del ruido de fondo de la propia película. Un buen oído quizá todavía lo note en la palabra reparada. El ejemplo de audio de la charla no está incluido en esta página. Diapositiva 21 .

121.title: IA dentro de las herramientas que ya usamos
121.content: La IA también puede trabajar a través de las herramientas que ya usamos. Las empresas que las fabrican la están incorporando, tanto para control y gestión como para procesamiento. DaVinci Resolve 21.1 permite que asistentes de IA lo operen directamente, Premiere Pro tiene un AI Assistant que trabaja dentro del proyecto, y Avid ha mostrado IA agéntica para Media Composer. Las herramientas de restauración pueden funcionar de la misma manera. Diapositiva 22 .

122.title: Dónde están los límites ahora
122.content: . | Lo que mejor ha funcionado es conservar la propia imagen de la película y dejar que el modelo agregue solo lo que falta: el color, un hueco, una palabra. | El color se mantiene a lo largo de un plano cuando referencias aprobadas guían todo el plano, ya sea a través de un modelo de video o del pequeño adaptador. | Lo que más ayuda es el control. Los bordes, el movimiento con seguimiento y el registro mantienen al modelo pegado a la película, no a su propia idea de ella. | En el flujo de trabajo de color, un modelo pequeño aprende de fotogramas maestros aprobados y completa el plano, así que el modelo grande no tiene que ejecutarse en cada fotograma. | Lo que todavía tiene que mejorar es la resolución y la duración. Los modelos siguen viendo una imagen reducida, de unos diez segundos a la vez. | Nada de esto se hace con un clic. Requiere paciencia, y un restaurador que decida qué es aceptable y que diga qué se generó. | . Hace un año, incluso hace un par de meses, nada de esto era posible.

128.title: Do CopyCat aos modelos de pesos abertos
128.content: Minha pesquisa começou com o CopyCat, dentro do Nuke. A ideia é treinar um modelo pequeno para cada filme a partir de quadros correspondentes de duas cópias: a digitalização danificada e uma cópia melhor do mesmo filme, que mostra o resultado que queremos. Foi isso que apresentei no ano passado em Roma, e continua sendo a minha base de comparação. Mas o método precisa dessa cópia melhor para aprender, e é uma plataforma fechada, feita para efeitos visuais. Desde então, os modelos de pesos abertos, aqueles que qualquer pessoa pode baixar e rodar, ficaram bons o bastante para imagem, vídeo e voz em uma única estação de trabalho. As pessoas já usam esses modelos para “restaurar” fotos antigas e filmes caseiros, mas quase sempre fora do arquivo. Então a minha pergunta é: como podemos restringi-los para que se tornem úteis para o trabalho que realmente precisamos fazer? . Slide 3 .

129.title: Mascarar versus recuperar
129.content: A maioria das ferramentas de restauração usa filtros espaciais e temporais. Elas pegam imagem emprestada do mesmo quadro, ou dos quadros ao redor, e quando não há nada limpo para copiar, elas interpolam. O slide mostra o Dry Clean no Phoenix em Point Blank (1967); as marcas vermelhas são o que ele detectou e removeu. Essas ferramentas conseguem esconder poeira, riscos e cintilação, e preencher dois ou três quadros faltantes. Mas não conseguem trazer de volta o que se perdeu. Sendo honestos, a restauração digital sempre foi sobre mascarar, não sobre recuperar. Por isso, a IA na restauração não é algo completamente novo. O que ela nos dá é uma forma de enfrentar problemas que antes não eram viáveis, técnica ou financeiramente, trabalhando com a digitalização do jeito que ela está. Em muitos arquivos, principalmente na América Latina e no Sudeste Asiático, essa digitalização desbotada é tudo o que resta de um filme. 130.title: As limitações

Eles suavizam o grão e os detalhes finos, ou inventam detalhes novos. A imagem parece mais nítida, mas deixa de parecer filme. | Resolução e duração. Nos meus testes, os modelos de vídeo locais trabalharam em torno de 768 × 432 pixels e só conseguiam acompanhar cerca de dez segundos de cada vez. O resultado dele é combinado com a luma, ou seja, o brilho, da digitalização original, então a resolução, o grão e os detalhes continuam como estavam. O fluxo de trabalho está documentado aqui. 132.title: Criando uma referência sintética
132.content: E o que acontece quando não existe referência? Você cria uma: um quadro de cor aprovado para cada plano. Eu chamo isso de referência sintética, e faço com o Qwen Image Edit, um modelo de imagem de pesos abertos da Alibaba. A minha primeira tentativa foi guiá-lo com uma leader lady, a mulher dos quadros de calibração no início de um rolo. Não funcionou. Esses modelos não entendem significado como nós, então, em vez de pegar só a cor, o modelo misturou as duas imagens e a mulher acabou entrando no plano. Eu chamo isso de contaminação semântica. Uma carta de cores simples funcionou melhor, depois que eu a desfoquei levemente. Ela guia a cor sem dar ao modelo mais nada para copiar. Depois veio o prompt, que é a forma de conversar com o modelo. Fiz um pequeno concurso, que chamei de America's Next Top Machine Learning Model: dezenas de prompts e centenas de quadros de teste, em sete rodadas com sete filmes desbotados. Um prompt só passava de uma rodada se oito de cada dez quadros fossem aceitáveis. A fileira de baixo do slide mostra um quadro desbotado de Counter Attack, um filme chinês de 1976, com três dos finalistas. O vencedor, Clara, é o que eu mais uso, mas também uso os outros, dependendo do plano. Da referência sintética eu fico só com a cor. O brilho continua vindo da digitalização. 133.title: Mantendo a cor estável ao longo de um plano
133.content: Conseguir um quadro convincente já não é a parte difícil. Se você simplesmente rodar o modelo 24 vezes por segundo, não funciona, porque esses modelos não são determinísticos: cada execução é um pouco uma roleta. Cada quadro recebe uma interpretação ligeiramente diferente, e a cor cintila. O slide 8 mostra uma cena de dança de Obsession em que cada quadro foi recuperado separadamente. Observe o vestido da mulher à direita e o fundo. Cada quadro, sozinho, é uma interpretação razoável, mas juntos eles não combinam. Um bom quadro é uma miniatura. Uma restauração precisa que o plano inteiro seja coerente consigo mesmo. Isso é consistência temporal, e foi o maior obstáculo. 134.title: Tornando o processo mais rápido: H3 e ControlNet
134.content: Eu tinha uma cor que se mantinha, mas o processo demorava demais. No fim de julho, a MiniMax lançou o H3, um modelo de vídeo muito bom com imagens de referência. Em uma única passada, ele leva a cor aprovada por um trecho inteiro de um plano. Sozinho, porém, o H3 se afasta da imagem e perde a geometria. Então eu tive que rodá-lo em trechos curtos e fazer com que todos combinassem, o que significava mais processamento e mais tempo. Depois, em agosto, a Alibaba PAI lançou um ControlNet para o H3. Um ControlNet é uma forma de direcionar o que o modelo faz; este fornece ao modelo as bordas de cada quadro, o que ajuda a manter a geometria e o movimento do próprio filme. Eu fico só com a cor e a coloco sobre o brilho original, para que o grão, a aspereza e até a sujeira permaneçam. Deixados por conta própria, esses modelos querem mudar tudo e deixar a imagem com aspecto de plástico. Assistir · 0:13 Slide 11 · Counter Attack: H3 + ControlNet, finalizado com o adaptador Temporal CbCr . A cor vem do H3 com o ControlNet, e é finalizada com o adaptador Temporal CbCr, explicado na próxima seção. Escolhi este plano porque ele é difícil: muito movimento, uma multidão que muda o tempo todo e uma panorâmica rápida no meio. O que funcionouA cor se mantém durante todo esse movimento, e a geometria continua igual à do original. LimitaçõesOlhando de perto, há um pouco de dominante de cor nas sombras. A minha cópia estava a 30 quadros por segundo com a cadência quebrada, então foi difícil extrair quadros limpos dela, e o adaptador precisa de quadros bem alinhados. 135.title: O adaptador Temporal CbCr
135.content: Esta é a ideia por trás do meu trabalho com o CopyCat, levada para fora do Nuke para que a pesquisa possa rodar em uma plataforma aberta. CbCr são os dois canais de cor de uma imagem de vídeo, mantidos separados do brilho. Eu rodo o H3 ou o TeleStyle uma ou duas vezes, dependendo da duração do plano, e fico só com os quadros que passam na revisão. Eu os chamo de professores. Eles não precisam cobrir o plano inteiro, desde que a geometria deles esteja alinhada com a imagem. Um modelo pequeno, com menos de um milhão de parâmetros, aprende a cor do plano a partir dos professores em poucos minutos. Depois, ele preenche os quadros que não têm professor e mantém a cor estável ao longo de todo o plano. No slide 12, o primeiro e o terceiro quadros não têm professor, e o segundo e o quarto têm. Assistir · 0:07 Slide 13 · Unman, Wittering and Zigo (1971): adaptador Temporal CbCr . Uma cena de coral, com a fonte desbotada à esquerda e o resultado do adaptador à direita. Neste plano, o H3 não se alinhou com a imagem, então todos os professores vieram do TeleStyle. Eles cobriram 101 dos 164 quadros, e o adaptador preencheu o restante. O treinamento em si levou cerca de um minuto e meio (88,5 segundos). O que funcionouEle preserva tudo o que está no original: a sujeira, a aspereza do filme. Até o vitral atrás do coral se mantém consistente durante toda a panorâmica. LimitaçõesO adaptador só é tão bom quanto os seus professores, e precisa de quadros bem alinhados. 136.title: Upscaling por difusão*
136.content: * Na palestra usei o nome anterior, diffusion upscaling. Este trabalho sobre o plano inteiro de Tinterillo chama-se agora Diffusion Full Reconstruction. Diffusion Upscaling é uma ideia nova e separada para aumentar a resolução e o detalhe do vídeo com referências. Até aqui, o modelo só acrescenta cor, e a digitalização mantém a sua própria imagem. Mas às vezes o elemento que sobreviveu não tem informação suficiente para uma restauração tradicional. Nossas ferramentas pegam emprestado do mesmo quadro ou dos quadros ao redor, e quando todos os quadros estão danificados, não sobra nada para pegar emprestado. O upscaling por difusão permite que um modelo de vídeo reconstrua a imagem a partir do que sobreviveu, seguindo a sua estrutura e o seu movimento. El Tinterillo sobrevive apenas como uma cópia em 16mm danificada e uma telecinagem mais limpa, mas suave, cortada nas bordas e com a cadência estranha das telecinagens daquela época. Suavizei o 16mm com um filtro de mediana e depois combinei os dois, com a telecinagem por dentro e o 16mm em volta. Isso dá um contorno aproximado para guiar a geometria, mas o filtro também remove os detalhes finos. Então, para definir como a imagem deveria ficar, fiz outras referências sintéticas com o ChatGPT Images. O MiniMax H3, no modo de referência, usa então essas referências, com o clipe da telecinagem para o movimento, para gerar cada trecho do plano. Assistir · 0:26 Slide 15 · El Tinterillo: upscaling por difusão, a escada . A digitalização original em 16mm está à esquerda, e o resultado que aprovei está à direita. Foi preciso um longo processo de iteração para chegar aqui. O que funcionouA imagem nesta digitalização não tem salvação com as ferramentas tradicionais. O H3 preenche essas lacunas e reconstrói a imagem, seguindo a estrutura e o movimento do original. LimitaçõesO resultado é parcialmente sintético: o modelo inventa detalhes finos que o filme já não tem, e isso precisa ser declarado. O modelo trabalhou em 768 × 432. Ainda há um salto de brilho no primeiro quadro, e os rostos e os detalhes finos continuam fracos. Algumas pessoas vão chamar isso de heresia, e até certo ponto é. Eu mesmo não chamaria isso de restauração de filme propriamente dita. Mas, com um material como este, não vejo outro caminho, e talvez precisemos abrir a cabeça para o que a restauração pode ser. comparação 1920 × 756 · 26 s · 24 fps . | Baixar o vídeoMP4 · 1920 × 756 · 62.1 MB | Abrir no Google Drive | . 137.title: Reconstrução por difusão*
137.content: * Na palestra usei o nome anterior, diffusion reconstruction. Este trabalho de reparação de lacunas e partes de fotogramas chama-se agora Diffusion Healing: sobrevive muita imagem utilizável e a difusão repara perdas específicas. Diffusion Full Reconstruction é o projeto separado de regeneração do plano inteiro. Às vezes a imagem não está danificada, ela simplesmente não existe mais: são quadros que faltam no único elemento sobrevivente. Isso acontece muito com nitrato, quando um trecho em decomposição foi cortado para não danificar o resto do rolo. Ferramentas como Phoenix, DIAMANT ou DaVinci Resolve conseguem preencher dois ou três quadros faltantes com fluxo óptico. Em uma lacuna mais longa, o movimento começa a parecer errado, porque elas só conseguem interpolar o que sobreviveu. Na palestra, o exemplo é uma lacuna de 15 quadros em um negativo de câmera cujo som ainda sobrevive, então a lacuna precisa ser preenchida para manter imagem e som juntos. Rastreei os atores do último quadro antes da lacuna até o primeiro quadro depois dela, e levei esse movimento pelos quadros faltantes: são os esqueletos do slide 16. Depois, o modelo de vídeo VACE, da Alibaba, gerou a imagem, guiado por esse movimento, somente dentro da lacuna. O que funcionou, e as limitações. Os quadros gerados se sustentam bem, e todos os quadros originais permanecem intactos. A limitação de resolução do slide 4 continua valendo, e o que é gerado precisa ser declarado. O trecho mostrado no slide 17 não está incluído nesta página. Slides 18–19 .

138.title: Combinando fontes e depois reconstruindo
138.content: Quando vários elementos sobrevivem, normalmente cada um está danificado em lugares diferentes. Na palestra, mostrei isso em um filme mudo que sobrevive como uma cópia em nitrato e uma cópia de segurança em diacetato. Juntas, elas cobrem a maior parte do filme, mas em alguns pontos o nitrato se decompôs e a cópia de segurança também não tem esses quadros. Primeiro, eu junto os dois elementos. Eles tinham cor, deformação e enquadramento diferentes, então cada quadro de um é alinhado ao outro pelas suas características e deformado até se encaixar. Depois, uma única correção de tom, ajustada nos quadros correspondentes mais limpos, dá aos dois a mesma aparência. Em seguida, cada quadro vem do elemento que sobreviveu sem danos. Uma linha do tempo do plano funciona como um mapa disso: de qual elemento vem cada quadro e onde nenhum dos dois sobreviveu. Nesses quadros, eu mascaro apenas as áreas danificadas, e o Wan VACE 14B, modelo de vídeo da Alibaba, reconstrói só essas áreas. A imagem que sobreviveu continua original, porque não queremos substituir um quadro inteiro só porque uma parte dele está danificada. O que funcionou e as limitações. O resultado se sustenta bem, e tudo o que sobreviveu fica intacto. Foi um teste de trabalho em resolução reduzida, não uma restauração nativa em HD. O exemplo da palestra não é mostrado nesta página. Slide 20 .

139.title: Recuperação de diálogos
139.content: A mesma ideia vale para o som: uma palavra muito distorcida pode ser reconstruída a partir da própria voz do ator. Usei o Fish Audio S2 Pro, um modelo de fala de pesos abertos, rodando localmente. Ele recebe alguns segundos de diálogo limpo do mesmo ator, tirados do filme, cerca de dez segundos neste caso, e as palavras exatas. Ele gera muitas tomadas da fala inteira. O reconhecimento de fala e a comparação de voz ajudam a classificá-las, mas quem decide é a escuta. Depois, só a parte danificada volta para o lugar, cerca de um terço de segundo aqui. Todo o resto é a trilha sonora original. Limitações. O resultado do modelo saiu tão limpo que não se misturava, então acrescentei um pouco do ruído de fundo do próprio filme. Um ouvido treinado ainda pode perceber isso na palavra reparada. O exemplo de áudio da palestra não está incluído nesta página. Slide 21 .

140.title: IA dentro das ferramentas que já usamos
140.content: A IA também pode trabalhar por meio das ferramentas que já usamos. As empresas que as fabricam estão incorporando a IA, tanto para controle e gerenciamento quanto para processamento. O DaVinci Resolve 21.1 permite que assistentes de IA o operem diretamente, o Premiere Pro tem um AI Assistant que trabalha dentro do projeto, e a Avid já mostrou IA agêntica para o Media Composer. As ferramentas de restauração podem funcionar da mesma forma. Slide 22 .

147.title: From CopyCat to open-weight models
147.content: My research started with CopyCat, inside Nuke. The idea is to train a small model for each film from matching frames of two copies: the damaged scan, and a better copy of the same film that shows the result we want. That's what I presented last year in Rome, and it's still my baseline. But it needs that better copy to learn from, and it's a closed platform built for visual effects. Since then, open-weight models, the ones anyone can download and run, have become good enough for images, video and voice on a single workstation. People already use them to “restore” old photos and home movies, but almost always outside the archive. So my question is: how do we constrain them so they become useful for the work we actually need? . Slide 3 .

148.title: Masking versus recovery
148.content: Most restoration tools use spatial and temporal filters. They borrow picture from the same frame, or from the frames around it, and when there's nothing clean to copy, they interpolate. The slide shows Dry Clean in Phoenix on Point Blank (1967); the red marks are what it detected and removed. These tools can hide dust, scratches and flicker, and bridge two or three missing frames. But they can't bring back what is lost. If we're honest, digital restoration has always been about masking, not recovery. So AI in restoration isn't something completely new. What it gives us is a way to take on problems that weren't technically or financially possible before, working with the scan as it is. In many archives, especially in Latin America and Southeast Asia, that faded scan is the only thing left of a film. 149.title: The limits
149.content: As I see it, there are three main limits. | They weren't made for film. These models were built to create or edit born-digital images. They smooth away grain and fine detail, or invent new detail. The picture looks sharper, but it stops looking like film. | Resolution and length. In my tests, local video models worked at around 768 × 432 pixels and could only follow about ten seconds at a time. 150.title: Reference-based colour recovery
150.content: Let's start with what already works. A small model trains on matching pairs of frames: the faded source, and a reference that still carries the colour. That reference can be a telecine, a DVD, another print, or the original negative wherever the two overlap. The model only learns colour. Its output is combined with the luma, the brightness, of the original scan, so resolution, grain and detail stay as they were. The workflow is documented here. 151.title: Creating a synthetic reference
151.content: So what happens when there's no reference? You create one: an approved colour frame for each shot. I call it a synthetic reference, and I make it with Qwen Image Edit, an open-weight image model from Alibaba. My first try was to guide it with a leader lady, the woman on the calibration frames at the start of a reel. It didn't work. These models don't understand meaning the way we do, so instead of taking only the colour, the model mixed the two images and the woman ended up in the shot. I call that semantic contamination. A plain colour chart worked better, once I softly blurred it. It guides the colour without giving the model anything else to copy. Then came the prompt, which is how you talk to the model. I ran a small contest, which I called America's Next Top Machine Learning Model: dozens of prompts and hundreds of test frames, over seven rounds on seven faded films. A prompt only survived a round if eight out of ten frames were acceptable. The bottom row of the slide shows a faded frame from Counter Attack, a Chinese film from 1976, with three of the finalists. The winner, Clara, is the one I use most, but I use the others too, depending on the shot. From the synthetic reference I keep only the colour. The brightness still comes from the scan. 152.title: Keeping colour steady through a shot
152.content: Getting one convincing frame is no longer the hard part. If you just run the model 24 times a second, it doesn't work, because these models aren't deterministic: every run is a bit of a roulette. Each frame gets a slightly different interpretation, and the colour flickers. Slide 8 shows a dance scene from Obsession where every frame was recovered on its own. Watch the dress of the woman on the right, and the background. Each frame is a fair interpretation by itself, but together they don't agree. One good frame is a thumbnail. A restoration needs the whole shot to agree with itself. That's temporal consistency, and it was the biggest hurdle. 153.title: Making it faster: H3 and ControlNet
153.content: I had colour that held together, but it took far too long. At the end of July, MiniMax released H3, a video model that is very good with reference images. In one pass, it carries the approved colour through a whole section of a shot. On its own, though, H3 drifts from the picture and loses the geometry. So I had to run it in short sections and make them all agree, which meant more processing and more time. Then in August, Alibaba PAI released a ControlNet for H3. A ControlNet is a way to steer what the model does; this one feeds it the edges of every frame, which helps keep the film's own geometry and movement. I keep only the colour and put it on top of the original brightness, so the grain, the roughness, even the dirt, stay. Left on their own, these models want to change everything and make it look plasticky. Play · 0:13 Slide 11 · Counter Attack: H3 + ControlNet, finished with the Temporal CbCr adapter . The colour comes from H3 with the ControlNet, and it's finished with the Temporal CbCr adapter, explained in the next section. I chose this shot because it's hard: a lot of movement, a crowd that keeps changing, and a fast pan in the middle. What workedThe colour holds through all that movement, and the geometry stays the same as the original. LimitsLook closely and there's some tint in the shadows. My copy was 30 frames per second with a broken cadence, so getting clean frames out of it was hard, and the adapter needs properly aligned frames. 154.title: The Temporal CbCr adapter
154.content: This is the idea behind my CopyCat work, taken out of Nuke so the research can run on an open platform. CbCr are the two colour channels of a video picture, kept separate from its brightness. I run H3 or TeleStyle once or twice, depending on the length of the shot, and keep only the frames that pass review. I call them teachers. They don't have to cover the whole shot, as long as their geometry lines up with the picture. A small model, with fewer than a million parameters, learns the colour of the shot from the teachers in minutes. Then it fills in the frames that have no teacher and keeps the colour steady across the whole shot. On slide 12, the first and third frames have no teacher and the second and fourth do. For this shot, H3 didn't line up with the picture, so all the teachers came from TeleStyle. They covered 101 of the 164 frames, and the adapter filled the rest. Training itself took about a minute and a half (88.5 seconds). What workedIt keeps everything in the original: the dirt, the roughness of the film. Even the stained glass behind the choir stays consistent through the whole pan. LimitsThe adapter is only as good as its teachers, and it needs frames that line up properly. 155.title: Diffusion upscaling*
155.content: * The talk used the earlier name diffusion upscaling. This whole-shot Tinterillo work is now Diffusion Full Reconstruction. Diffusion Upscaling is a separate new idea for reference-based video resolution/detail enhancement. So far, the model only adds colour and the scan keeps its own picture. But sometimes the surviving element doesn't carry enough information for a traditional restoration. Our tools borrow from the same frame or the frames around it, and when every frame is damaged, there's nothing left to borrow. Diffusion upscaling lets a video model rebuild the picture from what survives, following its structure and movement. El Tinterillo survives only as a damaged 16mm print and a telecine that is cleaner, but soft, cropped and with the strange cadence of telecines from that time. I smoothed the 16mm with a median filter, then combined the two, with the telecine inside and the 16mm around it. That gives a rough outline to guide the geometry, but the filter also removes the fine detail. So, for how the picture should look, I made more synthetic references with ChatGPT Images. MiniMax H3, in reference mode, then uses those references, with the telecine clip for the movement, to generate each section of the shot. Play · 0:26 Slide 15 · El Tinterillo: diffusion upscaling, the stairs . The original 16mm scan is on the left, and the result I approved is on the right. It took a long process of iteration to get here. What workedThe picture in this scan is beyond saving with traditional tools. H3 fills those gaps and rebuilds the picture, following the structure and movement of the original. LimitsThe result is partly synthetic: the model invents fine detail the film no longer carries, and that has to be declared. The model worked at 768 × 432. There's still a jump in brightness on the first frame, and faces and fine detail remain weak. Some people will call this heresy, and to a degree it is. I wouldn't call it proper film restoration myself. But with footage like this, I don't see another way, and we may need to open our minds to what restoration can be. 1920 × 756 comparison · 26 s · 24 fps . | Download the videoMP4 · 1920 × 756 · 62.1 MB | Open in Google Drive | . 156.title: Diffusion reconstruction*
156.content: * The talk used the earlier name diffusion reconstruction. This gap and partial-frame repair work is now Diffusion Healing: substantial usable picture survives, and diffusion repairs specific losses. Diffusion Full Reconstruction is the separate whole-shot regeneration project. Sometimes the picture isn't damaged, it's gone: frames missing from the only surviving element. This happens a lot with nitrate, when a decaying section was cut out so it wouldn't damage the rest of the reel. Tools like Phoenix, DIAMANT or DaVinci Resolve can bridge two or three missing frames with optical flow. Across a longer gap, the motion starts to feel wrong, because they can only interpolate what survives. In the talk, the example is a 15-frame gap in a camera negative where the sound still survives, so the gap has to be filled to keep picture and sound together. I tracked the actors from the last frame before the gap to the first frame after it, and carried that movement through the missing frames: those are the skeletons on slide 16. Then Alibaba's VACE video model generated the picture, guided by that movement, only inside the gap. What worked, and the limits. The generated frames hold up well, and every original frame stays untouched. The resolution limit from slide 4 still applies, and what is generated has to be declared. The clip shown on slide 17 isn't included on this page. Slides 18–19 .

157.title: Combining sources, then reconstructing
157.content: When several elements survive, each one is usually damaged in different places. In the talk I showed this on a silent film that survives as a nitrate print and a diacetate safety copy. Together they cover most of the film, but in some places the nitrate has decayed and the safety copy is missing those frames too. First, I bring the two elements together. They had different colour, warping and framing, so each frame of one is matched to the other by its features and warped into place. Then one tone correction, fitted on the cleanest matching frames, gives both the same look. After that, each frame comes from whichever element survives undamaged. A timeline of the shot works as a map of this: which element each frame comes from, and where neither survives. In those frames I mask only the damaged areas, and Wan VACE 14B, Alibaba's video model, reconstructs only those. The surviving picture stays original, because we don't want to replace a whole frame just because part of it is damaged. What worked, and the limits. It holds together well, and everything that survives stays untouched. It was a working test at reduced resolution, not a native HD restoration. The example from the talk isn't shown on this page. Slide 20 .

158.title: Dialogue recovery
158.content: The same idea applies to sound: a word that has been badly distorted can be rebuilt from the actor's own voice. I used Fish Audio S2 Pro, an open-weight speech model, running locally. It's given a few seconds of the same actor's clean dialogue from the film, about ten seconds in this case, and the exact words. It generates many takes of the whole line. Speech recognition and voice comparison help rank them, but listening decides. Then only the damaged part goes back in, about a third of a second here. Everything else is the original soundtrack. Limits. The model's output was so clean that it didn't blend in, so I added some of the film's own background noise. A good ear may still hear it in the repaired word. The audio example from the talk isn't included on this page. Slide 21 .

159.title: AI inside the tools we already use
159.content: AI can also work through the tools we already use. The companies that make them are building it in, for control and management as well as processing. DaVinci Resolve 21.1 lets AI assistants operate it directly, Premiere Pro has an AI Assistant that works inside the project, and Avid has shown agentic AI for Media Composer. Restoration tools can work the same way. Slide 22 .

179.title: Experimental Film Restoration with Machine Learning
179.content: Faded colour brought back, decayed nitrate healed, films beyond repair rebuilt, with open-weight models running on local hardware. The film's own picture stays the record; the model only supplies what is lost. Where things stand Run it yourself Reveal Obsession (1976), the ballroom. A trailer faded to solid red, 254 frames of dancing and a moving camera; the colour recovered on the scan's own brightness at 2048 × 1556. Record Independent research by Fabio Bedoya, done alongside commercial restoration work in London, into what open-weight AI models can do for the archives that can't afford the commercial route, and how far those models can be trusted. If you think about it, digital restoration was never really about recovery. The usual tools copy information from the frames around the damage and mask it. These models can put back what was actually lost, and that is new. It is also where the risk is, so the rule is the same in every area here: start from the scan, keep its picture, use a model only for what is missing, and write down what the model did. Nothing is automatic. Every result is reviewed at full size before it goes up, and every example has a record of its source, models and settings.
