191.title: Provenance and Metadata for ML Restoration

192.title: Motivation
192.content: If a model touched the picture, whoever comes after should be able to see what was trained, on what, with what settings, and run it again. That is the whole point of the record: a future restorer or an archive can understand the work and check it. A result you can’t check is just a nice picture.

193.title: Core Principles
193.content: Four things to do every time. Say that a model was involved: tag the output with the tool, the method and the date. Say where the picture came from: the source and reference elements, the scan details, and who gave permission. Say what the model learned from: the shots and frames, the steps, the model size, the checkpoint. And say what kind of recovery it was: colour (with a reference or without one), spatial, or both.

194.title: Minimum public record
194.content: For every published result, record: . | the source element and scan used; | every visual reference and the right to use it; | the model, workflow, prompt, seed, and relevant settings; | whether the output is reference-based, reference-free, spatial, chroma-only, or combined; | the training frames and checkpoint when a project-specific model was trained; | the processing date and the person or institution that made the final call; | a plain statement of what is generated interpretation and what is historical evidence. | . Keep this record with the output even when the same fields are also written into the image file. Files get converted; sidecars get lost; one of them should survive. IPTC Digital Source Type . Tag the output with trainedAlgorithmicMedia or compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia, so that anyone reading the file knows a model was involved. EXR Metadata (Nuke) . A ModifyMetaData node before the Write puts the record into the EXR itself, where Resolve and archival systems can read it: . metadata = nuke.nodes.ModifyMetaData() metadata['metadata'].fromScript(""" set exr/MLProcessing "CopyCat Color Recovery" set exr/RecoveryType "Reference-Based Color" set exr/SourceElement "16mm positive print" set exr/ReferenceSource "PAL DVD 2003" set exr/ModelCheckpoint "checkpoint_60000" set exr/IPTCDigitalSourceType "trainedAlgorithmicMedia" """) . Sidecar files . Keep a small machine-readable record and a plain-language note beside the renders. At minimum, name the source and reference elements, the model and checkpoint, the frames used for training, the processing date, and the person or institution responsible for the restoration decisions. Resolve integration . Resolve reads the EXR metadata in its Metadata panel. Map the keys to Description, Scene/Shot/Take, Keywords, Creator, Rights and Dates, and use Batch Change for the fields that are the same across clips.

204.title: Where things stand
204.content: October 2026, after SEAPAVAA in June and FIAT/IFTA in São Paulo. The short version: if you keep the film’s own picture and use a model only for what is missing, every kind of loss tried this year has come back on at least one whole shot, and most on several. What it takes is time, passes and someone reviewing, not a breakthrough that hasn’t happened yet. Area by area, what works, what doesn’t, and what you can run yourself.

205.title: 1. Faded colour recovery
205.content: Whole shots with hard motion, at the scan’s full resolution: a crowd with a fast pan (385 frames), a ballroom with a moving camera (254 frames at 2048 × 1556), a quarry in six sections (681 frames), a waterfront with fast hands, all from the same faded copy of Counter Attack, and the balanced-source route end to end on a commercial. One colour frame checked at full size, MiniMax H3 with the Fun ControlNet to carry it through the shot, the frames that pass review teaching the Temporal CbCr adapter, and the adapter colouring every frame. Only the colour is taken; brightness, grain and damage stay the scan’s. Some shots still need a second pass. The target is three out of four new shots right first time, and it is close but not there. Deep shadows keep a tint on the hardest shots. The video models see a reduced picture, about 768 × 576 and ten seconds at a time, which is why shots are done in sections and why you waste inference. And the colour is an interpretation unless a surviving reference confirms it. You can run the single-frame kit (one faded frame to one colour frame, in Comfy Cloud or locally, no Python) and the palette still from the balanced-source kit without a GPU. The rest of the balanced kit does a whole shot end to end on a local card. See faded colour recovery.

206.title: 2. Temporal CbCr
206.content: With a historical reference (a DVD, a telecine, another print) a small model learns the colour from the matching frames: Candy Candy from a PAL DVD, Frontier Experience from a telecine. With a synthetic reference, about a hundred reviewed frames teach the adapter, which trains in 90 seconds and colours the rest of the shot: Unman, Wittering and Zigo. The adapter is the finishing step of the whole-shot colour results above, and it has done a 25-minute film. Lining up a historical reference is still partly by hand, and a synthetic reference is only as good as the frames that get through review. New examples are being made and will be added to the page. The Nuke template for CopyCat is on the releases page, with the CopyCat workflow guide; the adapter code is in the balanced-source kit. See Temporal CbCr.

207.title: 3. Diffusion healing
207.content: Nitrate decay healed on a whole shot of Knights of the Trail: in the 18 damaged frames the actor stays the film’s and only the ruined background is generated, the other 206 frames are untouched, and every generated pixel is on record. A 16mm reversal shot with the emulsion breaking up across the whole frame (the Wong flute players) healed from one storyboard sheet, with the film’s own drumming kept. A fifteen-frame hole in a camera negative (Poison Pen, 1939), with the sound running on, is being filled with the actors’ movement tracked across the gap. The healed shots are at working size (640 × 512, 768 × 560); the pass at the scan’s full resolution is a separate step. The Wong shot stops at a good result at working size, to be finished with conventional restoration. The fastest, thinnest movement, a drumstick, is still better kept from the film than generated. And none of it is one click. You can run the second-pass kit. See diffusion healing.

208.title: 4. Diffusion reconstruction
208.content: A whole reel of El Tinterillo, a film that survives only as a heavily damaged 16mm print and a soft telecine, rebuilt shot by shot to one look: the stairs (624 frames) and three more shots of 410, 422 and 176 frames with the same method. The last still has its lip movement to do. The result is labelled as a reconstruction, with detail the film no longer holds. Small faces and lips are the limit, because the model works at 768 × 432; the next pass targets articulation. Video upscalers, Wan VACE driven by the source and a CopyCat detail model were all tried on this material and dropped. You can run the stairs kit. See diffusion full reconstruction.

209.title: 5. Black-and-white colourization
209.content: Fifteen shots finished, whole shots at full resolution with the original brightness untouched, the colour fitted to the stock that recorded the film: The General (a garden scene and a pan on a locomotive) and six other public-domain films of the 1920s. Skin on the earliest shots, some foliage, and soft, low-detail sources are the weak points. More complex movement and subjects are the next tests. The palettes are interpretations, and the route is not published yet. See black-and-white colourization.

210.title: 6. Diffusion Upscaling
210.content: Research idea. Reference-based video upscaling and basic resolution/detail enhancement, separate from whole-shot regeneration and selective healing. No workflow, benchmark or result is qualified for the new project. Historical Tinterillo upscaling records remain Full Reconstruction evidence. See Diffusion Upscaling.

211.title: What can be reproduced
211.content: Every example on the site has a record of its source, route, models and settings, and the download kits reproduce four of them from the published files and say how closely (ΔE against the published result). Every graph is published laid out with notes that say what the step does and what should and should not happen on the footage, and as the API-format prompt the server runs. The graphs use built-in ComfyUI nodes only. The model file names, prompt, seed, steps, cfg and sampler are in the graph itself, and ComfyUI writes the whole graph into every PNG it saves, so a run is repeatable on another machine to within the models’ own run-to-run variation, which is small at a fixed seed but not zero.

212.title: Comfy Cloud
212.content: Not everyone has a GPU, so the two still-frame graphs (the single-frame kit and the balanced kit’s palette still) open and run in Comfy Cloud as they are, with the bf16 Qwen Image Edit model from Cloud’s own library. The published recipe uses the fp8mixed model, which has to be imported from Hugging Face (Creator plan or higher), and the bf16 model gives a visibly different colour on some surfaces (ΔE 2.67 on the palette still). The video steps (MiniMax H3, Wan VACE) and the Python steps run locally.

213.title: Next
213.content: The original-resolution pass for the healed shots, starting with Knights of the Trail. Lips on the El Tinterillo reel. One app that runs the current colour route on new shots, which is possible now but still needs too many decisions to be left alone. And the healing and reconstruction routes as self-contained graphs, beyond the second-pass and window kits that are published.

240.title: Preparation and Alignment: Stages 0–2
240.content: This page covers the first stages of the CopyCat workflow: Resolve export, Nuke project setup, dataset curation, alignment and the shared crop. Then continue with building the colour target. If the reference is hard to match (a telecine, a broadcast master, a DVD with different edits), see Preparing Reliable Training Pairs: lining things up reel by reel, shot by shot and frame by frame, and throwing out the pairs you can’t trust. The whole workflow, start to finish.

241.title: Stage 0: Resolve Export + Nuke Project Setup
241.content: Before anything else, make sure the scan keeps as much of the picture as it can: no clipping, no automatic white balance, no creative grade baked in, no compressed low-bit-depth intermediates. The scan is what you have to work with, and whatever it lost the model can’t get back. For the background, see Digitization: First Scan, Last Chance. Source and Reference Preparation . What matters is whether the reference has the colour, not whether it is newer, sharper or higher resolution. A soft DVD with the right colour is a better reference than a sharp copy with the wrong one. Source preparation: . | Balance the source technically, not creatively: neutral blacks and whites, nothing that looks like a grade. | Take out severe flicker, dirt, splice flashes and instability first. The model will learn them otherwise. | If the grain gets in the way of learning the colour, degrain the source for training only. Write down the settings and keep the original plate; the grain comes back with the original luma at the end, because only the colour is taken from the model. | If the whole scan has a strong cast, from dye fade or from the scanner, give it a neutral, technical pre-balance first. For the background on magenta dye fade and channel imbalance, see Why Faded Scans Turn Magenta. | . Before (raw faded scan) After a neutral pre-balance Candy Candy: the magenta cast neutralised in Resolve before going into Nuke. Reference preparation: . | Clean enough that transfer artefacts don’t mislead the model. | A light denoise, deband or median takes care of dust, compression noise and banding. Don’t change the geometry and don’t warp in time. | . Geometry and stabilisation: prefer cleanup that leaves the geometry alone. If you have to stabilise or reframe, do exactly the same thing to both exports. Resolve Export . | Put both sources in one timeline. Turn off retimes, effects and per-clip grades. | Line the reference up with the source in Edit/Inspector (Translate/Scale/Rotate). Letterbox or pillarbox is fine; what matters is that the framing doesn’t move. | Use one colour-management path for both elements and write it down. If you train in display-referred Rec.709, give both exports the same display transform and check their range before they go anywhere near CopyCat. | Check that resolution, pixel aspect, frame range and rate, and channel set (RGB only, no alpha) match. | Note any global offsets (scale, translate, rotate); you will want them later. | . Rules: . | Same frame range, framing, and resolution. | No creative grading. | Fix interlacing, cadence problems, and decode issues before export. | . QC checklist: . | Dimensions, frame ranges, and pixel aspect match | Channel sets match (RGB), values in 0–1 when read into Nuke | No retimes or extra colour transforms that crept in | . Nuke Project Setup . Project settings: . | Colour management: the OCIO/ACES configuration the project uses. | Working space: one working space for the whole project, written down. | Viewer process: the display transform that matches the display you review on. | . Read node settings (both Source and Reference): . | Set the input transform to match what Resolve actually exported. | An archival ACES master and a display-referred training file are two different things; don’t label one as the other. | . Verify: . | Flip the viewer between Source and Reference; they should look consistent under the chosen ODT. | Both branches should have the same ingest transform. | . ACES and Color Management Reference . The domain this workflow trains in: display-referred Rec.709. The same transform on source and reference, check the range, and build the YCbCr target from those matched files. Log, as an alternative: it works in theory, but it is a lot slower and, in testing, the colour came out worse. Only if the footage demands it. Don’t clamp linear ACES: reading ACES 2065-1 and clamping it to [0–1] crushes the highlights and spoils the colour mapping. If you start from ACES masters, go to display-referred first. Input and Target have to be in exactly the same domain with the same transforms. Don’t mix linear on one branch with display-referred on the other. Write nodes (delivery): . | Archival: Write.colorspace = ACES - ACES2065-1 (AP0), EXR 16-bit half (ZIP/DWAA). | Review/proxy: Rec.709 ODT → ProRes/H.264. Note the viewing intent and the ODT. | . Resolve interop: . | Write down the exact ACES/OCIO configuration and transforms the project uses. | Keep archival masters separate from display-referred training exports. | Keep frame size, pixel aspect ratio, channel set, and frame range identical between paired training files. | .

242.title: Stage 1: Dataset Curation
242.content: Train on a small set of frames that represent the shot, not the whole sequence. A handful of good pairs beats hundreds of doubtful ones. Building paired training examples in Nuke. Selection Criteria . | Source frames: intact luma and texture, typical grain, as little gate weave as possible. Avoid frames that are mostly motion blur unless the reference has the same blur. | Reference frames: the same shot and timecode when you have it, or a well-made stand-in. Avoid heavy compression, burned-in subtitles or logos, and grades that wander. | Leave out: pairs where one side has something the other doesn’t (a flash, a splice mark). The model can’t reconcile those. | . Pair Counts . | Scope | Pairs | Notes | . | Shot | 4–9 | Add more if convergence stalls | . | Scene | 12–24 |   | . | Sequence | 24–64+ | Scale with variability | . For a short range (say frames 20–60), take a frame at the beginning, two in the middle and one at the end. Coverage . Cover the range of what is in the shot: . | Lighting: warm/cool, day/night, interior/exterior | Subjects: skin tones, foliage/sky, fabrics, neutrals | Extremes: deep shadows, specular highlights, saturated primaries | . Pairing Rules . | In time: the same frame index or timecode. If it is one frame out, take the frame where the static structure overlaps most. | In space: the same resolution and orientation. Overscan and crop have to be shared; what is left over is dealt with in Stage 2. | Colour space: both sides under the same transform (a Rec.709 export, say) so the values stay in 0–1. | . Nuke Build . | Create a FrameHold per selected index on both Source and Reference branches. | Assemble ordered stacks with AppendClip: one for Source (Input), one for Reference (Target). | Keep a staging AppendClip upstream of the one the PostageStamp nodes point at, so you can reorder pairs without breaking anything. | Check each pair with a viewer wipe or Merge (difference). You are judging geometry and alignment here, not colour. | Label the pairs consistently and keep a table of indices and timecodes, so you can find your way back later. | . Documentation . | Write down the shot, the pair indices and why you chose them. | Note whether the reference is direct (a telecine, a DVD, a print) or constructed, and where it came from. | Flag the compromises (compression, leftover parallax) so you remember to look for them during training. | .

243.title: Stage 2: Alignment
243.content: The point of this stage is that Source and Reference end up differing only in colour: pixel-accurate alignment, and the same crop on both. Auto and manual alignment paths inside the template. Strategy . | One global solve with F_Align on a conservative central ROI. Don’t iterate on it. | Check it straight away with Merge (difference). If edges or geometry are still showing, switch to a manual Transform with keyframes. | Keep a Dissolve so you can flip between the auto and manual paths quickly. | . Merge (difference) in the viewer: geometry and edges should be close to black. Colour differences are expected, that is the whole point; only a structural misalignment is a problem. Crop and Subtitle Handling . | Take the black borders and overscan off both branches. Don’t train on anything that isn’t picture. | Keep burned-in subtitles and logos out. Where you can’t, animate a shared crop. | Give Source and Reference the exact same crop (clone or link the node) so the pixels correspond. | . Shared crop keeping both branches in the same live picture area. Nuke Build . | Compare Reference to Source with Viewer wipe and Merge (difference). | A Dissolve switches between the auto and manual paths. Keyframe it per frame (0 = auto, 1 = manual) once you have looked. | Auto path: F_Align with a conservative central ROI, one global solve (Translate/Scale/Rotate/Perspective). Don’t chase parameters. | Manual path: Transform (translate/scale/rotate) keyed as needed. Judge it with Merge (difference). | Reference crop, last: add a Crop on the aligned Reference to take off overscan and anything that comes and goes. Keep it bypassed while solving and turn it on at the end. Keep this node; it gets cloned or linked in Stage 3. Don’t crop the Source here. | . Verification Checklist . | Merge (difference) shows only colour differences; geometry and edges close to black. No Grade or colour correction at this point. | No shimmer at the borders or corners when flipping between Source and Reference. | The reference crop takes off overscan and mattes without hiding what you align by. | . Troubleshooting: gate weave and parallax on a warped reference several generations down can mean a lot of manual Transform keyframing. It takes time; there is no shortcut.

244.title: Next: Stage 3, the colour target
244.content: The ground-truth target takes its brightness (Y) from the Source and its colour (Cb/Cr) from the Reference. Convert both branches to YCbCr before channel recombination. Shuffle node used to build the ground-truth target. CopyBBox gives Source and Ground Truth the same bounding box before they go into CopyCat. Continue with building the colour target, then training, inference and review. Common Failure Modes . | Training on an unstable source (flicker, dirt, severe imbalance). | Trusting a bad reference just because it is higher resolution. | Keeping misaligned frames in the dataset. | Leaving borders, subtitles, or overlays inside the training area. | Expecting one model to solve every shot in a difficult sequence. | .

249.title: Temporal CbCr
249.content: This is the oldest idea in this research and still the most reliable one. If something survives that has the colour, a DVD, a telecine, another print, a negative that overlaps the faded print for a few shots, you can teach a small model the colour from the overlap and let it colour the rest. You take only the chroma from the model and combine it back with the luma of the scan, so the result is the original resolution with everything nice about it, plus the colour. And because we are not very sensitive to the resolution of colour, a standard-definition reference is enough. The first version of this ran in CopyCat in Nuke, and that still works; the Nuke template is below. But Nuke is a closed platform meant for VFX, and research needs something it can build on, so the job now has its own small model: the Temporal CbCr adapter. It trains on one shot in about 90 seconds, it has done a 25-minute film end to end, and it is what finishes most of the whole-shot results on this site. Reveal Unman, Wittering and Zigo (1971), the choir. A trailer faded to magenta, 164 frames with a pan; 101 frames that passed review taught the adapter, which coloured the rest in a minute and a half. Record

250.title: Two kinds of reference
250.content: The reference can be historical: a better copy of the same frames survives, it lines up with the scan, and it teaches the colour. Then the result is a recovery. Or the reference can be synthetic: nothing better survives, so an open model (MiniMax H3, Qwen Image Edit, TeleStyle) makes candidate colour frames, a person reviews them, and only the ones that pass become teachers. Then the result is an interpretation, and it is only as good as the frames that were let through.

251.title: How it works
251.content: First the reference has to line up with the scan, in time and in position, and that is checked by eye; cuts and changing speeds are where it goes wrong. Then the frames to learn from are picked: matching pairs from the historical reference, or the synthetic frames that passed. The adapter learns only the colour of that shot, which is why it trains in about 90 seconds, and then it runs over the whole shot. The colour holds from frame to frame with no flicker, at the scan’s full resolution. With a historical reference, CopyCat in Nuke does the same job, and the CopyCat workflow walks through it.

253.title: What works and what doesn’t
253.content: With a historical reference this is production ready. It has been used on commercial work where a faded print had to fill gaps in a negative, and it was quite good, quite straightforward. On Frontier Experience the adapter beat CopyCat on nine of sixteen test shots, and it is a lot faster. The adapter is also the finishing step for the whole-shot colour results on the colour recovery page: the crowd, the ballroom, the balanced-source shot all end with it. What is still by hand is the alignment. A DVD also brings its own grading and its own softness of colour, and the result inherits them. And a synthetic reference moves the whole question to the review: the model will happily learn a wrong colour if a wrong frame gets through. New examples for this page are being made and will be added as they are finished. A proper write-up of the adapter is coming.

257.title: Glossary
257.content: Terms used in the research on this site. Standard Nuke node names (Read, Write, Merge, Transform, Crop, etc.) are not redefined here; consult Foundry documentation for those. ACES 2065-1 . Linear AP0 scene-referred colour space for archival/exchange masters. Recommended delivery space with EXR half. Alignment . Pixel-accurate registration of Reference to Source, including crop, so the two differ only in colour. Chroma (Cb, Cr) . Colour-difference channels in YCbCr. In chroma recovery, these come from the Reference branch. CopyCat . Nuke node that trains a compact CNN using supervised Input/Target pairs assembled in the node graph. F_Align . Furnace alignment operator used as an automated first pass before manual Transform refinement. Film gauge . Physical film width (16mm, 35mm). Different gauges have distinct spatial characteristics and damage patterns. Film generation . Duplication stage (original negative, internegative, print, duplicate). Generational differences affect spatial quality. Ground truth (Target) . The desired output used as Target during training. For colour recovery: Source Y + Reference Cb/Cr. Hold-out frames . Frame pairs excluded from training, used only for validation. Inference . Nuke node that applies a trained .cat model to new frames/sequences. Internegative . Intermediate negative created from a positive element. Often higher spatial quality than distribution prints. Luma (Y) . Brightness channel in YCbCr. In chroma recovery, luma comes from the Source branch. MatchGrade . Nuke node for look matching. Used in these workflows as an optional baseline to compare against learned reconstruction. Provenance . The written history of a result: the sources, the steps and the settings, so that someone else can check it and run it again. Synthetic reference . A colour frame for a shot, made with an open model when no better copy of the film survives and checked at full size. It guides the colour of the shot, and the result is an interpretation. Teacher frames . The frames of a shot that pass review and are used to train the Temporal CbCr adapter for that shot. Telecine . Video transfer of a film element from earlier preservation workflows. May preserve cleaner sections despite lower resolution. Temporal CbCr adapter . A small model, trained for one shot, that learns its colour (Cb and Cr) from teacher frames and carries it through every frame while the scan keeps its own brightness. Training pair . A single supervised example: Input (degraded) and Target (ground truth) sharing identical content and alignment. YCbCr . Color model separating luma (Y) from chroma (Cb, Cr). Used to construct ground truth by recombining channels from Source and Reference.

259.title: Training, Inference, and Review
259.content: The last stages of the CopyCat workflow. Build the colour target first: Source Y with Reference Cb and Cr.

260.title: Stage 4: Train and monitor
260.content: Start with a modest model, and keep back a frame the model never trains on. That held-out frame is how you know whether it has learned the colour or just memorised the pairs. | Setting | Starting point | Review note | . | Model | Medium | Try Large only after pair quality and alignment are sound | . | Patch | 512 | Use 256 when the crop is limited, then expect more steps | . | Batch | 3 | Reduce only when memory requires it | . | Steps | 40,000 to 80,000 | Stop or carry on according to the held-out frame, not the loss alone | . | Checkpoints | Every 10,000 steps | Compare the same held-out material at each checkpoint | . | Contact sheets | About every 100 steps | Use them to spot divergence and memorisation | . A little geometric augmentation is fine when the composition allows it, and mild exposure variation can help. Don’t use anything that changes the colour relationships; colour is the thing the model is learning. The Progress tab shows loss and training crops over time. A held-out preview tells you more than the loss, because it is a frame the model hasn't seen. Check that input and target have the same range and bounding box. Their luminance should still be nearly identical.

261.title: Stage 5: Infer the source sequence
261.content: You train on a few pairs; you run the model on the whole source. | Read the original source in the same colour-management domain you trained in. | Apply the same live-area crop, but not the alignment transforms, which were only for training. | Repeat any preprocessing you did to the source for training. | Load the chosen .cat checkpoint in an Inference node. | Render 50 to 100 frames from around the shot before you commit to the full range. | Review motion, transitions, first and last frames, and shot joins. | Add new pairs only to fix something you actually saw go wrong, then test again. | . The trained model run over the whole source sequence. For archival renders, follow whatever the project delivers in. A common choice is 16-bit half-float EXR with ZIP or DWAA compression in ACES2065-1. Put the shot, the version and the model or checkpoint in the file name.

262.title: Final review
262.content: Compare the original and the recovered render in the same colour-managed Resolve project, with grades and effects off. Wipe, split screen or toggle the tracks, then watch the sequence at normal speed as well as frame by frame. Some things only show up at speed. | Protect in the source | Optional Resolve composite | Reject when | . | Luminance and detail | Color | Colour bleeds, flickers, changes identity, or contradicts evidence | . Scopes show you range, luminance and chroma changes, but they don’t tell you whether the result is good. That is decided by a person looking at it.

263.title: Record the delivery
263.content: Keep: . | the original scan and exact reference edition; | source and reference credits and permissions; | selected pair indices and alignment notes; | model, checkpoint, Nuke version, and colour-management settings; | short validation renders and rejected examples; | a note on the assumptions, what still isn’t right, and who made the final call. | . The provenance guide has a fuller record to follow.
